Novo Nordisk Foundation Center for Basic Metabolic Research and Department of Public Health, University of Copenhagen Copenhagen Denmark ([ROR:02s32fb62](https://ror.org/02s32fb62)) † Corresponding author ## Abstract Background:Comorbidity with type 2 diabetes (T2D) results in worsening of cancer-specific and overall prognosis in colorectal cancer (CRC) patients. The treatment of CRC per se may be diabetogenic. We assessed the impact of different types of surgical cancer resections and oncological treatment on risk of T2D development in CRC patients.Methods:We developed a population-based cohort study including all Danish CRC patients, who had undergone CRC surgery between 2001 and 2018. Using nationwide register data, we identified and followed patients from date of surgery and until new onset of T2D, death, or end of follow-up.Results:In total, 46,373 CRC patients were included and divided into six groups according to type of surgical resection: 10,566 Right-No-Chemo (23%), 4645 Right-Chemo (10%), 10,151 Left-No-Chemo (22%), 5257 Left-Chemo (11%), 9618 Rectal-No-Chemo (21%), and 6136 Rectal-Chemo (13%). During 245,466 person-years of follow-up, 2556 patients developed T2D. The incidence rate (IR) of T2D was highest in the Left-Chemo group 11.3 (95% CI: 10.4–12.2) per 1000 person-years and lowest in the Rectal-No-Chemo group 9.6 (95% CI: 8.8–10.4). Between-group unadjusted hazard ratio (HR) of developing T2D was similar and non-significant. In the adjusted analysis, Rectal-No-Chemo was associated with lower T2D risk (HR 0.86 [95% CI 0.75–0.98]) compared to Right-No-Chemo.For all six groups, an increased level of body mass index (BMI) resulted in a nearly twofold increased risk of developing T2D.Conclusions:This study suggests that postoperative T2D screening should be prioritised in CRC survivors with overweight/obesity regardless of type of CRC treatment applied.Funding:The Novo Nordisk Foundation (NNF17SA0031406); TrygFonden (101390; 20045; 125132). ## Introduction Colorectal cancer (CRC) is the third most common cancer worldwide (Araghi et al., 2019), and the incidence rate (IR) is still increasing (Arnold et al., 2017 ). The same applies to the global IR of type 2 diabetes (T2D). The association between CRC and T2D is well established, as patients with T2D have approximately 30% increased risk of developing CRC (González et al., 2017), and T2D is known to negatively influence the prognosis of CRC (Mills et al., 2013). Furthermore, some studies even show an increased T2D risk in CRC survivors (Singh et al., 2016; Xiao et al., 2021). Fortunately, survival after a CRC diagnosis is steadily improving due to early detection, diagnostic precision, and more advanced cancer treatment; and today, more than 70% of non-metastatic CRC patients are alive after 5 years (Colorectal, 2019). Accordingly, it becomes increasingly important to identify CRC patients at risk of developing long-term health problems like T2D in order to initiate preventive strategies or treatment (Xiao et al., 2021). The underlying mechanisms behind the increased T2D risk in CRC survivors are poorly understood. However, shared lifestyle-related risk factors such as obesity, physical inactivity, and unhealthy diet may play a role (Nano et al., 2020; Maddatu et al., 2017; Lega and Lipscombe, 2020). Another explanation may be treatment-induced hyperglycemia. Prior studies showed that treatment with adjuvant chemotherapy can induce hyperglycemia and development of T2D in CRC patients (Xiao et al., 2021; Jo et al., 2021; Feng et al., 2013). Moreover, glucocorticoid, administered to alleviate side effects of chemotherapy, may impair glucose homeostasis and thus increase the risk of T2D (Lee et al., 2021; Jeong et al., 2016). In addition to the drug-induced metabolic disturbances, a recent study revealed that the type of CRC surgery per se is associated with diverging risk of T2D (Jensen et al., 2018). A previous nationwide Danish study revealed that patients who had undergone left-sided colon resection for CRC and other colonic illnesses had an increased risk of developing T2D, whereas this risk was unaltered in patients who had undergone right-sided colonic resections compared with a control group (Jensen et al., 2018). However, this study lacks essential information on the role of potential modifying factors like body mass index (BMI), treatment with chemotherapy, etc. Along the same line, in a population of non-CRC patients, Lee et al. published that patients who had undergone right-sided or transversal colonic resections had a reduced risk of developing T2D compared with a matched non-colectomy control group (Wu et al., 2021). These findings raise an intriguing question of whether the risk of developing T2D in CRC survivors may be casually affected by the type of CRC surgery. Possible explanations of this side-specific risk modification include removal of different enteroendocrine cell types resulting in gut changes that is important for insulin secretion and action and for appetite regulation as well as changes in the microbiome, but causality remains to be investigated further (Holst et al., 2016; Lin et al., 2019; Palnaes Hansen et al., 1997). In the present study, we tested the hypothesis whether different types of surgical cancer resection and oncological treatment have an impact on risk of developing diabetes in CRC survivors. For this purpose, we used a nationwide register to compare the frequency of diabetes development in CRC patients who had undergone right-sided colectomy, left-sided colectomy, or rectal resection with and without chemotherapy, when adjusting for potential modifying factors like BMI, etc. ## Materials and methods ### Study population The study was based on information from Danish nationwide health registers. All data are recorded with reference to a civil registration number, which is a unique personal identification number assigned to all Danish residents. This number permits accurate linkage of recorded information at the personal level (Pedersen et al., 2011). The study population was identified through the Danish Colorectal Cancer Group (DCCG) database, which contains prospectively collected and validated data on all patients with CRC since 2001, including data on patient’s characteristics, diagnostics, and treatment (Klein et al., 2020). The degree of patient inclusion in the database is high (>95%) and thus adequately represents the population of Danish CRC patients undergoing cancer resections (Klein et al., 2020). We included all CRC cancer patients undergoing cancer surgery between 1 May 2001 until 31 December 2018 (Figure 1). Patients with unspecified surgery or total colectomy were excluded as these procedures are not standard treatment for CRC. Additionally, individuals diagnosed with type 1 diabetes (T1D) either before or after surgery were excluded, along with those diagnosed with T2D preoperatively or within the first 2 weeks postoperatively, as the last group probably represents patients with preoperatively unknown pre-existing prediabetes or diabetes. ![Figure 1.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89354/elife-89354-fig1-v1.jpg) ### Exposure Patients were subdivided into six groups according to the surgical procedure and whether the patients had received chemotherapy or not. The group ‘right-sided colonic resection’ (Right) included patients with cancer in coecum, ascending colon, or the oral part of colon transversum, the group ‘left-sided colonic resection’ (Left) included patients with cancer in the anal part of colon transversum, descending colon, and sigmoid colon, and the group ‘rectal resection’ (Rectal) included patients with rectal cancer. Information regarding chemotherapy was limited to whether the patient had received chemotherapy (Chemo) or not (No-Chemo). Based on the combination of surgical procedures and chemotherapy, the study population was divided into six groups: Right-No-Chemo, Right-Chemo, Left-No-Chemo, Left-Chemo, Rectal-No-Chemo, Rectal-Chemo. Radiation therapy is only part of standard treatment for rectal cancer, and therefore this oncological modality was restricted to Rectal patients (Rectal-No-Radiation vs. Rectal-Radiation). Finally, a sub-analysis was made comparing all colonic resected patients (All Colon) with all rectal resected (All Rectal). ### Outcome The primary outcome was first-time diagnosis of T2D after different types of CRC cancer surgery and chemotherapy. Patients were followed from date of surgery until time to T2D diagnosis, emigration, death, or the end of follow-up (31 December 2018), whichever came first. Individuals with T2D were identified from data in the Danish National Patient Register (comprising information on diagnoses during all hospital contacts in Denmark), the National Prescription Registry (comprising information on all prescriptions filled at any pharmacy in Denmark), and the Danish National Health Service Register (comprising information on podiatrist services) as described by Carstensen et al., 2011. Diabetes is defined as the second occurrence of any event across three types of inclusion events: (1) Diabetes diagnosed during hospitalisation, (2) diabetes-specific services received at podiatrist, and (3) purchases of glucose lowering drugs. Thus, if a patient developed transient T2D during chemotherapy treatment, it will only be an inclusion event if they purchase of glucose lowering drugs. Individuals were classified as having T1D if they had received prescriptions for insulin combined with a diagnosis of type 1 from a medical hospital department. Otherwise, diabetes was classified as type 2 (Isaksen et al., 2023). ### Statistical analysis Descriptive data was presented as means with standard deviations (SD) for continuous variables and proportions (n, %) for categorical variables. Crude IR (number of T2D diagnoses by person-time at risk) were calculated for the six groups (type of surgery±chemo), and characterised by preoperative variables (sex, age, BMI, smoking, alcohol status, American Society of Anesthesiologists physical status classification score [ASA], and treatment with radiotherapy in rectal cancer patients). Unadjusted and adjusted Cox regression analyses were used to calculate hazard ratios (HRs) for developing T2D after different types of surgery with and without chemotherapy (using Right-No-Chemo as a reference group), after radiation therapy among Rectal resected (using Rectal-No-Radiation as reference), and after overall type of surgery (All Colon [ref] vs All Rectal). The adjusted analyses were performed stepwise by first adjusting for year of surgery, age at surgery, sex, and BMI (Model 1), then further adjusting ASA, smoking, and alcohol consumption (Model 2a), and lastly, further adjusting for chemotherapy (Model 2b) in the analyses on radiation therapy and overall type of surgery. Finally, the impact of BMI on the risk of developing of T2D was investigated within each of the six groups. BMI was categorised into four subgroups (18.5–24.9, 25–29.9, 30–34.9, and 35–39.9), and underweight (BMI<18.5) or severely obese (BMI≥40) subjects were excluded from these analyses due to low numbers. For each group (type of surgery±chemotherapy), the HR for developing T2D depending on BMI subgroups was calculated by using Cox regression analysis adjusted for age, sex, year of surgery, and ASA score using normal weight (BMI: 18.5–24.9) as the reference group. A sensitivity analysis was performed by restricting the inclusion period of surgery patients from 2001–2018 to 2010–2018, as baseline information was complete from 2010. All analyses were conducted using STATA version 16 (STATA Corp., College Station, TX, USA). p-Value of p<0.05 was considered statistically significant. Results were presented with 95% confidence interval (CI) when relevant. ## Results ### Baseline characteristics A total of 46,373 CRC patients without preoperatively recorded diabetes were found eligible for the study (Figure 1) and were divided into six groups: 10,566 Right-No-Chemo (23%), 4645 Right-Chemo (10%), 10,151 Left-No-Chemo (22%), 5257 Left-Chemo (11%), 9618 Rectal-No-Chemo (21%), and 6136 Rectal-Chemo (13%). Compared with the Right, the Left and Rectal groups were younger, more often men, and less often classified as ASA>II (Table 1). Those that had received chemotherapy were generally younger, less often classified as ASA>II, and as expected more often stage III/IV cancers than No-Chemo. **Table 1.** Baseline characteristics.

### Risk of developing T2D after radiation therapy among rectal resected patients Radiation therapy in the rectal resected groups had no impact on the IR of T2D (Table 2), and the unadjusted/adjusted HR of developing T2D was non-significant when comparing Rectal-No-Radiation patients with Rectal-Radiation patients (Table 3). ### The impact of BMI on development of T2D BMI had a strong association with T2D regardless of surgical resection and treatment with chemotherapy (Figure 2). The risk of developing T2D increased near twofold every time the BMI group increased one level, e.g., in the Right-No-Chemo group: HR 2.13 in BMI 25–30, HR 3.63 in BMI 30–35, HR 8.01 in BMI 35–40, compared with the reference BMI of 18.5–25. A similar pattern was observed within each of the other five groups, although a less pronounced impact of BMI was observed in the Left-No-Chemo group: HR 1.85 in 25–30, 2.93 in 30–35, 4.21 in 35–40 BMI group. ![Figure 2.](https://cdn.elifesciences.org/articles/89354/elife-89354-fig2-v1.jpg) ## Discussion This national cohort study demonstrated an IR of developing T2D after CRC surgery similar to previous studies (Singh et al., 2016; Jo et al., 2021). Comparing resection types, rectal cancer resected patients had a slightly lower risk of developing T2D when compared to colon cancer resected patients. Treatment with chemotherapy had no impact on T2D risk in any of the resection groups, and radiation therapy did not affect T2D risk either. Within each of the six groups (different types of surgery with and without chemotherapy), BMI was strongly associated to developing T2D, the risk increased almost twofold every time the BMI group increased one level. Only few studies have examined the risk of developing T2D after different kinds of colonic and rectal surgical procedures, and in contrast to the present study the following studies were not able to adjust for several confounders incl. preoperative BMI. Jensen et al., 2018 found a higher risk of T2D after the left-sided compared with the right-sided colonic resections, but, in contrast to the current study, patients operated for both non-malignant and malignant diseases were included. In support of side-specific effect of colonic resections, Wu et al., 2021 investigated a population of non-CRC patients and showed that right-sided and transversal colonic resections were associated with a reduced risk of T2D development compared with patients without colectomy. In contrast to both the abovementioned studies the most recent epidemiological study found an increased T2D risk after colectomy compared with small bowel resection in non-cancer patients, but when stratifying by resection type, they found no difference in T2D risk (Allin et al., 2022). In Denmark, the overall T2D prevalence (6.9%) (Diabetesforeningen, 2023), is lower than the global average in 2021 (10.5%) and also falls below the estimate of high-income countries (11.1%) (Sun et al., 2022). Similarly, the obesity rate of 20% aligns with other Scandinavian countries and is below that of most high-income nations (Ritchie and Roser, 2023). Obesity is one of the predominant factors in the development of T2D (Wang et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2014; Lee et al., 2018), and the linear increase in new-onset T2D with increased BMI reported in this study is well described in the literature (Easson Karin et al., 2022). It is important to emphasise that only preoperative BMI was included in the adjustments as post-surgery BMI information was not available and accordingly, weight trajectories after surgery could not be included in the analyses. It’s still unknown how body weight and body composition changes after different types of CRC resection, and thus it is not clear whether changes in weight in any groups play a role in diabetes development. Like our findings, Jensen et al., 2018 and Wu et al., 2021 found a tendency towards a decreased risk of T2D after rectal resection, although these findings were not statistically significant in the previous studies. Further studies are needed to elucidate the potential mechanism behind this finding. We found no impact of treatment with chemotherapy on T2D risk, which was a bit surprising. Prior studies indicated that treatment with chemotherapy may induce hyperglycemia, and especially the combined use of chemotherapy and glucocorticoid, administered to alleviate side effects of chemotherapy, may have synergistic effects on later diabetes risk (Hwangbo et al., 2018). In the study period of the present study, different types of chemotherapy have been part of the standard treatment of colon and rectum cancer respectively, and knowledge regarding the specific effects of each drug on glucose homeostasis is sparse (Ariaans et al., 2015). In most cases CRC patients included in the study will however have been treated with the chemotherapy 5-fluorouracil (Feng et al., 2013). In a recent study a significant increase in glycemic variability, a precursor of T2D development, was found in non-diabetic early-stage colon cancer patients during 5-fluorouracil and capecitabine chemotherapy treatment (Mandolfo et al., 2022). Moreover, Feng et al. showed a 10% increased risk of developing T2D in CRC patients during and after treatment with adjuvant 5-fluorouracil. They argued that 5-fluorouracil could induce toxicity in B-cells leading to hyperglycemia (Feng et al., 2013). Similarly, Lee et al., 2021 revealed an impairment in glucose homeostasis in both breast cancer and CRC patients treated with chemotherapy and glucocorticoid following treatment. Nonetheless 65% of the newly diagnosed T2D cases remitted 6 months after discontinuation of chemotherapy, suggesting that chemotherapy is a reversible diabetogenic factor (Lee et al., 2021). Thus, in summary, treatment with chemotherapy may primarily induce transient effects on glucose homeostasis in CRC patients. In contrast to the lack of influence of chemotherapy treatment, it was not surprising that radiation therapy had no impact on diabetes risk in our study. Due to the strong negative prognostic effects of comorbidity with T2D on CRC outcomes, identifying CRC patients at increased risk of developing T2D is of great clinical importance. Our study did not support a role of cancer surgery with left-sided colonic resection or treatment with chemotherapy in T2D development in CRC survivors. However, in line with existing literature we found BMI to be strongly associated with T2D development. A core strength of the present study is the use of a nationwide database, allowing inclusion of large numbers of CRC patients treated with different types of CRC resections, providing valid real-life data regarding with close to complete coverage and long-term follow-up and a register-based approach to identify individuals with T2D. We were able to adjust for several confounders such as BMI, alcohol consumption, and smoking, which has been a limitation in previous studies (Jensen et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021). The limitation of the present study includes that information on BMI and other risk factors for developing T2D were only available preoperatively, eliminating the possibility of exploring an impact of BMI trajectories after cancer treatment until the T2D diagnosis (Winkels et al., 2016). Secondly, information on dose, length of treatment, and type of chemotherapy were not available. Thirdly, information on physical activity, diet, medication, and comorbidities, apart from the ASA score, were not available. In addition, our findings are limited by the register-based data collection method. Clinical well-designed mechanistic investigations are warranted to establish whether left-sided CRC resection per se drives metabolic alterations leading to an increased risk of T2D. In summary, we report a slightly increased risk of developing T2D after CRC treatment with colonic resection compared with rectal resection, whereas chemotherapy had no impact on new-onset T2D. Within each surgical subgroup, BMI at time of surgery was strongly associated to developing T2D. This study suggests that postoperative diabetes screening should be prioritised in CRC survivors with overweight/obesity regardless of type of CRC treatment applied.

Summary:

In this study, the authors set out to determine whether colorectal cancer surgery site (right, left, rectal) and chemotherapy impact the subsequent risk of developing T2DM in the Danish national health register.

Strengths:

- The research question is conceptually interesting

- The Danish national health register is a comprehensive health database

- The data analysis was thorough and appropriate

-The findings are interesting, and a little surprising that there was no impact of chemotherapy on the development of T2DM

- The authors have addressed my previous clarifications and questions.

- Regarding the generalizability of this study, as the authors discuss the prevalence of T2DM and obesity are lower in Denmark than in a number of other high income countries. Therefore, similar studies in other populations would be of interest.

- The study includes individuals who filled a prescription for diabetes medication, so likely includes some individuals with transient hyperglycemia/steroid induced diabetes during chemotherapy, rather than those with new onset longterm T2DM.

Overall, the authors achieved their aims, and the conclusions are supported by their results as reported.

The results are unlikely to significantly impact clinical practice or T2DM screening in this population, however are of interest to the community.

results.result: The study utilized the Danish Colorectal Cancer Group database (>95% coverage) to identify 46,373 CRC patients without preoperative diabetes who underwent surgery between 2001-2018. Patients were divided into six groups based on surgical resection type (right-sided, left-sided, rectal) and chemotherapy status.
results.evaluation: Claims C14-C17 and C77-C83 describe a well-defined cohort with clear inclusion/exclusion criteria and appropriate group definitions. The high database coverage (>95%, C15) and nationwide scope (C68) provide strong epidemiological validity. The exclusion of patients with T2D within 14 days post-surgery (C80) appropriately addresses prevalent undiagnosed diabetes.

results.result: During 245,466 person-years of follow-up, 2,556 cases of T2D were diagnosed (IR: 10.4 per 1000 person-years). The IR was highest in Left-No-Chemo (11.3) and lowest in Rectal-No-Chemo (9.6). T2D incidence was consistently higher in males, patients with BMI≥25, and ASA>I across all groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C27 present descriptive epidemiology with appropriate confidence intervals. The observed patterns (higher IR in males, higher BMI, worse ASA scores) align with established T2D risk factors, supporting internal validity. However, the relatively small absolute differences in IR between groups (9.6-11.3 per 1000 person-years) suggest limited clinical significance.

results.result: Rectal resection was associated with a modestly lower risk of T2D compared to right-sided colonic resection in adjusted analysis (HR 0.86, 95% CI 0.75-0.98 for Rectal-No-Chemo vs Right-No-Chemo). When comparing all colon vs all rectal resections, rectal resection showed significantly lower T2D risk in both unadjusted and adjusted models.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C31 demonstrate appropriate statistical methodology with stepwise adjustment for confounders (age, sex, BMI, ASA, smoking, alcohol). The finding that only Rectal-No-Chemo reached statistical significance (C29) while other comparisons did not (C28) is appropriately reported. The effect size is modest (HR 0.86) but statistically significant. Adjustment for cancer stage did not change results (C31), strengthening the finding.

results.result: Treatment with chemotherapy had no impact on T2D risk in any of the resection groups when comparing patients who received chemotherapy versus those who did not within each surgical category.
results.evaluation: Claims C40, C66, and C74 consistently report null findings for chemotherapy effect. Table 3 shows non-significant hazard ratios for all chemotherapy comparisons (e.g., Right-Chemo vs Right-No-Chemo: HR 1.01, 95% CI 0.85-1.20, p=0.884). This contradicts prior literature expectations (C8, C56-C63) but is appropriately supported by the data. The lack of detailed chemotherapy information (C71) is a limitation but does not invalidate the null finding.

results.result: Radiation therapy in rectal cancer patients had no impact on T2D incidence rate or risk (unadjusted/adjusted HR non-significant when comparing Rectal-Radiation vs Rectal-No-Radiation).
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 report null findings for radiation therapy effect, supported by Table 2 and Table 3 data. The comparison is appropriately restricted to rectal cancer patients only (C84), as radiation is not standard for colon cancer. The non-significant HR (0.97, 95% CI 0.84-1.12, p=0.691 in Model 2b) provides clear statistical support.

results.result: BMI showed a strong, dose-dependent association with T2D risk across all surgical subgroups. The risk increased approximately twofold with each BMI category increase (e.g., Right-No-Chemo: HR 2.13 for BMI 25-30, HR 3.63 for BMI 30-35, HR 8.01 for BMI 35-40 vs reference BMI 18.5-25). A less pronounced effect was observed in the Left-No-Chemo group.
results.evaluation: Claims C34-C37 and C42 are strongly supported by Figure 2 data showing consistent dose-response relationships. The hazard ratios demonstrate clear monotonic increases with BMI categories across all six groups. The finding aligns with established literature (C52-C53, C67). The observation of a less pronounced effect in Left-No-Chemo (C37: HR 1.85, 2.93, 4.21) compared to Right-No-Chemo (C36: HR 2.13, 3.63, 8.01) is interesting but unexplained and warrants further investigation.

results.result: The study had several methodological limitations: BMI and other risk factors were only available preoperatively (precluding analysis of post-surgical weight trajectories), detailed chemotherapy information (dose, duration, type) was unavailable, and data on physical activity, diet, medication, and comorbidities beyond ASA score were not captured.
results.evaluation: Claims C70-C72 transparently acknowledge important limitations. The lack of longitudinal BMI data (C70) is particularly significant given that BMI is the strongest predictor identified (C34-C37). The absence of chemotherapy details (C71) limits interpretation of the null chemotherapy finding (C40). These limitations appropriately temper the conclusions and are honestly reported.

results.result: Prior studies showed conflicting results regarding surgery type and T2D risk: Jensen et al. (2018) found higher risk after left-sided vs right-sided resection; Wu et al. (2021) found reduced risk after right-sided/transversal resection vs no colectomy; Allin et al. (2022) found increased risk after colectomy vs small bowel resection but no difference when stratifying by resection type. Both Jensen and Wu found non-significant trends toward decreased T2D risk after rectal resection.
results.evaluation: Claims C43-C46 and C54-C55 accurately summarize prior literature, though the current study's findings (C29-C30) partially contradict Jensen et al. (C43) by not finding increased risk for left-sided resection. The current study's finding of lower risk for rectal resection aligns with trends in prior work (C54-C55) but achieves statistical significance. The discrepancies may relate to differences in study populations (CRC vs non-CRC patients) and adjustment for confounders.

results.result: Prior literature suggested chemotherapy (particularly 5-fluorouracil) and glucocorticoids may induce hyperglycemia and increase T2D risk, but 65% of chemotherapy-induced T2D cases remitted within 6 months of treatment discontinuation, suggesting transient effects. The authors infer that most patients in their cohort received 5-fluorouracil and that chemotherapy may primarily induce transient glucose homeostasis effects.
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 cite prior literature suggesting chemotherapy effects on glucose metabolism, but the current study found no long-term T2D risk from chemotherapy (C40). The inference that effects are primarily transient (C100) is reasonable given the remission data (C62) but remains speculative. The assumption that most patients received 5-fluorouracil (C99) is plausible but unverified due to lack of detailed chemotherapy data (C71). The discrepancy between prior studies and current findings requires mechanistic investigation.

results.result: The authors recommend prioritizing postoperative diabetes screening in CRC survivors with overweight/obesity regardless of treatment type, and call for mechanistic studies to investigate whether left-sided resection drives metabolic alterations. Possible mechanisms include removal of different enteroendocrine cell types affecting insulin secretion/action and microbiome changes, but causality remains unestablished.
results.evaluation: Claim C76 is a reasonable clinical recommendation supported by the strong BMI-T2D association (C34-C37) and the relatively minor impact of surgery type (C29-C30). Claims C101-C103 appropriately acknowledge that mechanistic understanding is lacking and call for further research. The proposed mechanisms (C102) are biologically plausible but speculative, as appropriately noted (C103).

results.result: The study employed Cox regression with stepwise adjustment (Model 1: year, age, sex, BMI; Model 2a: +ASA, smoking, alcohol; Model 2b: +chemotherapy) to calculate hazard ratios. T2D was identified using a validated algorithm requiring two events across hospitalization diagnoses, podiatrist services, or glucose-lowering drug prescriptions. BMI was categorized into four groups (18.5-24.9, 25-29.9, 30-34.9, 35-39.9), excluding underweight and severely obese patients. Sensitivity analysis restricted inclusion to 2010-2018 when baseline data were complete.
results.evaluation: Claims C85-C98 describe appropriate statistical methodology. The T2D identification algorithm (C86-C89) is validated and reduces misclassification. Cox regression with stepwise adjustment (C90-C93) appropriately controls for confounders. The exclusion of extreme BMI categories (C95) is justified by small numbers but may limit generalizability. The sensitivity analysis (C96) addresses data completeness concerns. Statistical significance threshold (C98) is standard. Overall, the methodology is sound.

results.result: Baseline characteristics differed between groups: Left and Rectal groups were younger, more often male, and less often ASA>II compared to Right groups. Chemotherapy-treated patients were younger, less often ASA>II, and more often had stage III/IV cancers compared to non-chemotherapy patients.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 describe expected baseline differences supported by Table 1. The differences reflect clinical practice (younger, healthier patients receive chemotherapy; more advanced cancers receive chemotherapy). These differences justify the adjusted analyses (C90-C93) and are appropriately controlled for in the statistical models.

results.result: The study adjusted for several confounders (BMI, alcohol, smoking) that were limitations in previous studies (Jensen et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2021).
results.evaluation: Claim C69 accurately identifies a strength of the current study. The ability to adjust for BMI is particularly important given its strong association with T2D (C34-C37). This adjustment was not possible in Jensen et al. (2018) or Wu et al. (2021), making the current study's findings more robust.

results.result: The incidence rate of T2D after CRC surgery (10.4 per 1000 person-years) was similar to previous studies (Singh et al., 2016; Jo et al., 2021).
results.evaluation: Claim C38 provides external validation by comparing the observed IR to prior literature. This consistency supports the reliability of the T2D identification algorithm (C86-C89) and the representativeness of the study population.

results.result: Denmark's T2D prevalence (6.9%) is lower than the global average (10.5%) and high-income country estimate (11.1%). Denmark's obesity rate (20%) aligns with other Scandinavian countries and is below most high-income nations.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C51 provide important context for interpreting the study's findings. The lower T2D prevalence and obesity rates in Denmark compared to global averages may limit generalizability to populations with higher baseline risk. This contextual information is appropriately cited and relevant for external validity considerations.

results.result: The study found that rectal cancer resected patients had a slightly lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes compared to colon cancer resected patients, with adjusted HR 0.86 (95% CI 0.75-0.98) for Rectal-No-Chemo versus Right-No-Chemo.
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted this finding without critique. The first reviewer stated the evidence is 'solid' and the second reviewer noted the findings are 'interesting' and that 'the authors achieved their aims, and the conclusions are supported by their results as reported.'

results.result: The study found that treatment with chemotherapy had no impact on type 2 diabetes risk in any of the resection groups.
results.evaluation: While reviewers found this result 'interesting, and a little surprising,' they raised concerns about methodology. The reviewer noted 'The study includes individuals who filled a prescription for diabetes medication, so likely includes some individuals with transient hyperglycemia/steroid induced diabetes during chemotherapy, rather than those with new onset longterm T2DM,' suggesting the finding may be confounded by inclusion of transient cases.

results.result: The study found that radiation therapy in rectal resected groups had no impact on the incidence rate of type 2 diabetes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question this finding. The overall assessment that 'the evidence supporting the claims of the authors is solid' and that 'conclusions are supported by their results' applies to this result as well.

results.result: BMI was strongly associated with type 2 diabetes development across all surgical subgroups, with risk increasing approximately twofold with each BMI category increase (e.g., HR 2.13 for BMI 25-30, 3.63 for BMI 30-35, 8.01 for BMI 35-40 in Right-No-Chemo group).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly accepted this finding without critique. The first reviewer stated the evidence is 'solid' and both reviewers acknowledged the study's conclusions are supported. This finding aligns with established literature, which reviewers implicitly accepted.

results.result: The study recommends that postoperative diabetes screening should be prioritized in colorectal cancer survivors with overweight/obesity regardless of type of colorectal cancer treatment applied.
results.evaluation: While the first reviewer stated this finding 'suggest[s] the need for postoperative type 2 diabetes screening,' the second reviewer noted 'The results are unlikely to significantly impact clinical practice or T2DM screening in this population,' indicating uncertainty about the clinical applicability of this recommendation. The concern about including transient hyperglycemia cases also affects this recommendation's validity.

results.evaluation: While reviewers did not explicitly discuss these specific limitations, they raised related concerns. The reviewer noted the study 'likely includes some individuals with transient hyperglycemia/steroid induced diabetes during chemotherapy,' which relates to the lack of detailed chemotherapy data. comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate the null finding for chemotherapy effect on T2D risk (C40, C66, C74). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the null result appropriately supported by data despite contradicting prior literature. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, raising methodological concerns that transient hyperglycemia cases may confound the finding, suggesting the null result may be artifactual rather than genuine.

Both evaluate the null finding for radiation therapy effect (C32, C33, C41). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate restriction to rectal cancer patients and clear statistical support. Peer reviewers accepted this finding without critique as part of their overall assessment that conclusions are supported by results.

Both evaluate the BMI dose-response relationship with T2D risk (C34-C37, C42, C67, C75). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed analysis of monotonic trends and notes unexplained variation between groups. Peer reviewers explicitly accepted this finding as solid evidence aligning with established literature.

Both evaluate study limitations (C70, C71, C72). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval praises transparent acknowledgment of lack of longitudinal BMI and chemotherapy details. Peer reviewers implicitly acknowledge these limitations through related concerns about transient hyperglycemia and generalizability, though they did not explicitly discuss these specific limitations.

Both evaluate the Danish population context and generalizability concerns (C47-C51). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes lower T2D prevalence and obesity rates may limit generalizability to higher-risk populations. Peer reviewers explicitly raised this concern, stating similar studies in other populations would be of interest.

Both evaluate the finding of lower T2D risk for rectal resection without chemotherapy (C29, C30, C39, C73). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate statistical methodology and modest but significant effect size. Peer reviewers found the evidence 'solid' and findings 'interesting,' explicitly accepting the result without critique.

Both evaluate descriptive epidemiology (C20-C27 overlap, plus C16-C17 in peer review). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate confidence intervals and alignment with established risk factors but limited clinical significance. Peer reviewers praised the population-based cohort and thorough data analysis without raising concerns about the descriptive findings.

Both evaluate the clinical recommendation for postoperative T2D screening (C76). OpenEval rates as SUPPORTED, finding the recommendation reasonable given strong BMI-T2D association. Peer reviewers rate as UNCERTAIN, with one reviewer supporting screening need but another stating results unlikely to significantly impact clinical practice, indicating disagreement about clinical applicability.

Both address cohort methodology and database quality. OpenEval (R1) evaluates cohort definition and inclusion/exclusion criteria (C14-C17, C77-C83, C68) as SUPPORTED. Peer reviewers (R7) praise the nationwide Danish registry (C68, C69) as a methodological strength, rating SUPPORTED. Both recognize the high-quality population-based design.

Both evaluate the ability to adjust for BMI as a study strength (C69). Both rate as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes this advantage over prior studies. Peer reviewers praised the comprehensive Danish database and thorough data analysis, implicitly acknowledging this methodological strength.

OpenEval evaluates prior literature on surgery location effects (C43-C46, C54-C55) as SUPPORTED, noting the current study partially contradicts Jensen et al. but aligns with other trends. No corresponding peer review evaluation found addressing these specific literature comparisons.
